title: 4 STORIES PEOPLE POSTED AT 3 AM
intro: Four people posted these stories in the middle of the night. None of them ever posted again. Stay until the last one. It's the one I still think about.

stories.title: Our night doorman gave me one rule: never take the stairs after 2 AM
lines: I moved into a twelve-floor building in October.
The night doorman, Walt, has worked there for thirty years.
On my first night he slid a sticky note across the desk.
It said: after two A.M., use the elevator. Always.
I laughed. He didn't.
Three weeks later, the elevator broke at two fifteen in the morning.
I live on nine. I took the stairs.
Floor four. Floor five. Floor six.
Then floor five again.
I thought I'd miscounted, so I kept climbing.
Floor five. Floor five. Floor five.
Every landing had the same scuff on the wall. The same flickering light.
And on every landing, the door to the hallway was open a little wider.
On the seventh time, someone was standing in the doorway.
He was wearing Walt's uniform. But he was facing the wall.
He said: you used the stairs.
I ran down instead of up. I don't remember how many floors.
I burst into the lobby, and Walt was at his desk, reading the paper.
He didn't look up. He just slid me a new sticky note.
It said: he likes you now. Don't use the elevator either.

stories.title: My smart TV keeps turning on to a channel that doesn't exist
lines: Every night at three A.M., my TV turns itself on.
Same channel every time. Channel zero.
My TV doesn't have a channel zero. I checked the settings.
The first night it was just my living room. Empty. Dark.
It looked like a live feed from somewhere near the ceiling.
I thought someone hacked a camera, so I searched the whole room.
There is no camera up there. There is nothing up there.
The second night, the feed showed my couch. With me on it. Watching.
The third night, the feed showed my couch. With me on it.
But I was in the kitchen, holding the remote.
On the screen, I slowly turned my head toward the hallway.
In the kitchen, I didn't move at all.
I unplugged the TV. I put it in the garage.
Last night, at three A.M., my phone lit up.
A notification from an app I never installed. Channel zero.
Live now. Your bedroom.

stories.title: I'm a night nurse. Room 312 has been empty for a year. The call light still turns on.
lines: I work nights on the third floor of a small hospital.
Room 312 has been empty since last winter. Broken heater, they said.
The bed is stripped. The door is locked. Only the head nurse has the key.
At 3:12 every night, the call light for 312 turns on.
Maintenance replaced the wiring twice. It still turns on.
The older nurses told me the rule on my first week.
Never answer 312. Turn the light off from the desk and keep working.
Last Tuesday I was alone on the floor. The light came on.
And this time, the intercom crackled.
A small, tired voice said: nurse, I'm cold. Can you bring a blanket?
I didn't answer. I turned off the light. It came back on.
Nurse, please. You promised you'd come back.
I have never been in that room. I have never promised anyone anything.
Then the voice said my name. My full name. The one only my mother uses.
I walked to 312. The door was unlocked. The bed was made.
And folded on the pillow was a hospital blanket with my name stitched in it.
The date on the tag was next winter.

stories.title: There's a door in my basement that wasn't there when we moved in
lines: We bought the house in June. The basement was one room. Four walls.
I know, because I painted all four of them myself.
In November, my daughter asked who lives behind the green door.
There is no green door in our house.
I went down to show her. And there it was.
A small green door in the wall I had painted white.
No dust. No hinges I could see. Just a brass knob, warm to the touch.
My husband said it must have been there all along.
He said we just never noticed it.
Last night I heard knocking. Three soft knocks. From the basement.
I went down with a flashlight. The knocks were coming from the green door.
From the other side, a voice I knew said: honey, it's me. Let me in.
It was my husband's voice.
I turned around to call him from upstairs.
He was already standing on the basement steps behind me.
Smiling. Holding the key.
So now I have to ask you something, and please answer fast.
Which one of them do I let in?
